analysis.one_liner: Sets government-set maximum prices for all prescription drugs sold in the United States.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its introduction: referred to three House committees with zero cosponsors, it received no hearing and no vote before the session ends in January 2027.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a new Prescription Drug Price Regulatory Commission that recommends a "fair price" for every approved prescription drug, which the Secretary of Health and Human Services would publish as a legal ceiling. Manufacturers charging more would face steep civil penalties, FTC and state enforcement, private lawsuits with triple damages, and the possibility of the government licensing their patents to competitors. Prices would be judged partly against what the same drugs cost in six other wealthy countries. The bill was referred to three House committees and never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients in the United States, including people on Medicare, Medicaid, private insurance, or paying cash — every prescription drug they buy would have a government-set ceiling price, backed by penalties, enforcement by the FTC and state attorneys general, and private lawsuits with triple damages for overcharges.
analysis.who_benefits_short: American patients buying any prescription drug

how_it_helps.text: Every prescription drug sold in the U.S. would have a government-published fair price that manufacturers must offer, factoring in production costs, therapeutic value, and prices in Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, and the U.K.

Manufacturers charging above the fair price would face civil penalties equal to 10 times the overcharge per unit, enforceable by the FTC, state attorneys general, and private citizens — who could recover triple damages or up to $50,000 per violation.

If a patent holder sells above the fair price or fails to meet patient demand, the government could license the patent to other producers; the President could also use Defense Production Act powers to expand domestic supply of a drug in shortage.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose revenue from the U.S. market — the world's most profitable — would be capped by formulas tied to production costs, research investment, and prices in Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, and the U.K.

drawbacks.text: Price controls on every prescription drug could reduce the revenue that funds research into new medicines; the bill itself acknowledges this by requiring the commission to weigh 'the return on investment that would provide adequate incentive to the manufacturer to continue research,' but critics would argue an appointed commission cannot judge that well.
The bill exempts the Commission from chapter 10 of title 5 of the U.S. Code (the federal administrative procedure law), reducing transparency and public input into how fair prices are set.

The Secretary can grant rolling 90-day waivers allowing prices above the fair price, and the fair price can be revised mid-year — giving agencies substantial discretion over whether the cap actually holds.
The bill would let the President use Defense Production Act powers to force domestic drug production, an unusually broad use of wartime economic authorities for ordinary drug supply.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is large: Americans pay far more than residents of peer countries for the same drugs, and a broad price cap with strong enforcement could lower out-of-pocket costs directly. The costs and risks are also real: price controls set below what it costs to develop a new drug could slow the arrival of new medicines, and this design — a single commission with almost every drug priced at once, using contested value measures, exempt from administrative-law review — concentrates enormous power in a small appointed body and could produce arbitrary results. And none of it will be tested: the bill never received a hearing or a vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees in May 2026, never received a hearing or a vote, and will die when the congressional session ends in January 2027.

narrative.text: Rep. Brad Sherman introduced H.R. 9040 on May 26, 2026; it was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Judiciary, and Financial Services committees the same day.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
No committee took any further action on the bill — no hearings, no markup, no vote — after the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers are better off: their pricing power is untouched, and Americans continue paying among the highest drug prices in the world.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug manufacturers and their pricing power

for.name: Rep. Brad Sherman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to three House committees; it was his proposal alone, with no cosponsors.

against.name: House committee chairs (Energy and Commerce, Judiciary, Financial Services)
against.role: Chairs of the three committees of referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after referral, leaving it to die in committee.

sides.party_line_note: No votes occurred, but the bill's sole sponsor is a Democrat and it drew zero cosponsors from either party, suggesting little cross-party appetite.

industries.note: The bill caps the price of every prescription drug at a government-determined fair price, enforced by civil penalties of 10 times the overcharge, FTC enforcement, state lawsuits, and patent licensing (march-in rights). This would sharply cut pricing power and revenue across the industry.
Pharmacies and dispensers would be required to provide the fair price to patients, which could squeeze margins on dispensing but also pass through lower acquisition costs.
Drug spending is a major driver of insurance premiums; caps on manufacturer prices would reduce the cost pressure that flows into premiums and employer health costs.

analysis.trajectory: The 119th Congress ends January 3, 2027. A bill with zero cosponsors that has received no committee action more than six months after referral will almost certainly die without a hearing or vote, as do the vast majority of introduced bills at this stage.
